description: For this challenge, I’m looking to build a creative and practical solution with people who are motivated, collaborative, and willing to contribute ideas and learn together. I’m particularly looking for teammates with skills in programming, AI/data analysis, UI/UX or web development, and data visualization.
summary:
NAWAR GeoAI is a free web platform that turns NASA climate data, soil type, and crop requirements into simple recommendations for farmers and gardeners in hot, water-scarce, remote areas. The user selects a country and city (or uses GPS), pins the exact farm location on a map, and enters the soil type, the previous crop, the starting season, and a goal: save water, maximize profit, or improve soil fertility.

Using the live NASA POWER API, the platform retrieves local temperature, rainfall, and solar radiation. It scores crops on climate fit, soil fit, and water need, builds three rotation strategies, and recommends a 3-season plan with the reason for each crop, water need, risk, and approximate return. The plan is then stress-tested under three climate scenarios, including +2°C warming and 20% less rainfall, to check how well it holds up.

Farmers in dry regions rarely have access to agricultural experts, so decisions based on guesswork waste scarce water and reduce yields. NAWAR GeoAI makes NASA data the core of the decision, plans across several seasons instead of one, and prepares users for a hotter, drier future. The platform is available in English and Arabic, runs in any browser with no installation, and lets users save multiple gardens.

Next, we plan to add NAWAR Field Node, a low-cost field sensor that brings ground measurements into the platform.
details:
Farmers in dry and remote regions deal with rising heat, scarce water, and irregular rainfall, and most have little access to agricultural experts. NAWAR GeoAI is a free web platform that supports the planting decision. Instead of suggesting one crop for one season, it plans three seasons ahead.

The user selects a country and city (or uses GPS) and pins the farm on a map. They enter the soil type, the previous crop, the starting season, and a goal: save water, maximize profit, or improve soil fertility. The platform retrieves temperature, rainfall, and solar radiation for that location from the NASA POWER API, then scores each crop in our database on climate fit, soil fit, water need, and the chosen goal. It builds three rotation strategies using agronomic rules, such as not repeating the same crop family and following cereals with legumes, and shows the best plan season by season with the reason for each crop, its water need, risk, and approximate return. Finally, it tests the plan under +2°C warming and 20% less rainfall [and shows a confidence level].

Benefits

The platform helps users choose crops that fit their local rainfall and temperature, use water more carefully, and protect the soil through rotation. The climate test shows how a plan performs in a hotter, drier year before anything is planted. It is free, runs in a browser without installation, works in English and Arabic, and explains each recommendation in plain language.

Intended impact

We want farmers and gardeners in dry regions to have science-based planting guidance even when expert advice is out of reach. The goal is less wasted water, lower risk of crop failure, and more reliable harvests as the climate changes.

Tools and technology

We built the site with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the map and Chart.js for the charts. Recommendations come from a rule-based scoring engine and a JSON crop database [based on FAO guidance]. We developed the code with Google Antigravity and hosted it with GitHub and GitHub Pages. SciSpace supported our research, Claude helped organize our text, and Canva and Google Gemini were used for slides, graphics, and the team logo. No hardware is used in the current version.

How it is creative

It combines multi-season rotation planning with climate stress testing in one simple tool, and it uses rules that can be explained instead of a black box. We also propose a low-cost field sensor, the NAWAR Field Node, to bring ground readings into the platform in the future.

Factors we considered

We chose NASA POWER because it covers any location, not only places with weather stations. We kept the interface simple and the results in plain language, so users with no technical background can follow them. We used explainable rules so each recommendation has a clear reason, and we added climate scenarios because a plan has to work in future conditions, not just today’s.

Future work

We plan to use real climate projections, add offline support and a mobile app, build the Field Node sensor, and pilot with real farms and agricultural experts.
